rv.q: It is still, in its small way, a revelation.
It’s a feast for the eyes, but a superficial take on a subject of infinite depth.
Not many plays can provide solid and varied entertainment and be potentially life-altering at the same time, but this is one of them.
It’s a tight, compact 90-minutes of real genius shared with an audience, both from its subject and its author.
For a genuinely remarkable theatrical experience, Mary Zimmerman’s scholarly and artistic masterpiece is well worth a visit.
There is no other playwright-director, alive or dead, like Mary Zimmerman.
It is astonishing and beautiful and meaningful.

What struck me about this deliberately staged production (deliberately choreographed would be an equally appropriate description) is how it felt as if we were uncovering Leonardo's musings while leafing through his papers.
But overall, da Vinci’s meditations on force, weight, perspective, and so much more still have the power to move and intrigue us...
As it turns out, the production, on a somewhat larger scale than the original, remains a testament to Zimmerman’s unique imagination, but it also comes with some problems.
Not having done so makes much of this show seem pointless and tiresome.

cn.t: Zimmerman's landmark visual spectacle dazzles with inventive staging and wondrous imagery, though critics note it lacks conventional plot or character development. Most praise the imaginative theatricalization of da Vinci's writings as magical and ingenious.
